title: Trie: Overview
summary: A prefix tree that stores strings efficiently by sharing common prefixes, enabling fast word and prefix searches.

sections.heading: What is a Trie?
sections.body:
A **trie** (also known as a **Prefix Tree**) stores a set of strings in a tree-like structure. Each node represents a character, and its children represent the next character in the string. Strings with a common prefix share the same nodes. For example, APPLE and APP share the nodes A→P→P.

Each node has a boolean `is_end_of_word` flag that marks whether the node represents the end of a word. This allows us to distinguish between stored words and prefixes.

sections.heading: When to Use a Trie
sections.body:
Tries are ideal for:
- **Prefix searches**: Check if any word starts with a given prefix
- **Auto-complete**: Suggest words based on a partial input
- **Spell checkers**: Validate words against a dictionary
- **Word games**: Efficiently store and search word lists

Tries beat hash sets when you need prefix queries—a hash set can only tell you if an exact word exists, but a trie can answer "do any words start with BA?" in O(L) time.

sections.heading: Operations
sections.body:
Tries support three main operations:
- **search(word)**: Returns `True` if the word exists in the trie. Start at the root and traverse down by following children matching each character. Check `is_end_of_word` at the final node.
- **insert(word)**: Adds a word to the trie. Traverse down, creating new nodes as needed, and mark the last node as `is_end_of_word = True`.
- **delete(word)**: Removes a word. Traverse to the last character, set `is_end_of_word = False`, then remove nodes that are not part of any other word.

All operations run in **O(L)** time, where L is the word length.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.body:
A `TrieNode` has:
- `children`: dictionary mapping characters to child `TrieNode` objects
- `is_end_of_word`: boolean marking end-of-word

The `Trie` class holds a reference to the root `TrieNode` and provides methods for search, insert, and delete.

approach: Use when you need prefix-based queries or autocomplete
When a hash set isn't enough—you need "starts with" not just "exact match"
String dictionary problems with common prefixes
Problems asking for longest common prefix or word break

complexity.time: O(L) for search/insert/delete, where L = word length
complexity.space: O(C) where C = total characters across all words

quiz.q: Why use a trie instead of a hash set for storing words?
options: A trie uses less memory than a hash set
A trie supports prefix queries efficiently, while a hash set only supports exact match
A trie has O(1) search time, while a hash set has O(L) search time
A trie automatically sorts words alphabetically
quiz.explain: The key advantage of a trie is efficient prefix queries. A hash set can only tell you if an exact word exists, but a trie can answer "do any words start with this prefix?" in O(L) time. Both have O(L) search for exact matches.

quiz.q: What does the is_end_of_word flag accomplish in a trie node?
options: It marks nodes that have no children
It distinguishes between stored words and prefixes of other words
It indicates the root of the trie
quiz.explain: The is_end_of_word flag distinguishes complete words from prefixes. For example, if we store APP and APPLE, the second P in APP needs is_end_of_word=True so search('APP') returns True, even though P has a child L.
